\chapter{What It Weighs, And How Much There Is}
\label{ch:el-kilo-y-el-litro}
\hlchaptermodality{359}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el metro, el gramo, el kilo, el litro and el peso, and put a number on a length, a weight and a volume.}

Complete ES-C359-peso: put a number and a unit on a length, on a volume and on a weight, and ask a shopkeeper for that much.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el metro]{el metro — one Spanish word, two Greek ancestors}

\label{lesson:ES-C359-metro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the kind}, then \emph{the brand}. (\emph{La clase}; \emph{la marca}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el número — what comes in front of it.
  \item la ciudad — what the other \emph{metro} runs under.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ME-tro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{tr} is one cluster, with a tapped \emph{r}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el metro} — \textquotedblleft{}the metre,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the underground.\textquotedblright{}

Those are two different words that happen to have arrived at the same shape, and keeping them apart is the point of this lesson.

The first is Greek \textbf{métron}, a measure. It is everywhere:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{diameter} is a measure across;
  \item \textbf{geometry} is earth-measuring, which is what it was for — resurveying Egypt after the Nile flooded;
  \item \textbf{symmetry} is measuring together;
  \item and every \textbf{-meter} on an instrument is a measurer.
\end{itemize}

When the French Revolution wanted a unit that belonged to nobody, it went to Greek and called it a \emph{mètre}.

The second \textbf{metro} is a train, and it has nothing to do with measuring. It is short for \emph{ferrocarril metropolitano}, and \textbf{metropolis} is \textbf{m\'{\={e}}tēr}, a mother, plus \textbf{pólis}, a city: the mother city, the one that sent out colonies.

So one Spanish word, two Greek ancestors, no relation between them.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The unit of length, and a warning that a short word can have two histories.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el metro}
  \item \emph{un metro}
  \item \emph{tres metros}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{métron} mean? (A measure.) And what is the \emph{metro} you ride short for? (\emph{Metropolitano} — the mother city.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el gramo]{el gramo — the same word as grammar}

\label{lesson:ES-C359-gramo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the brand}, then \emph{the metre}. (\emph{La marca}; \emph{el metro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la palabra — written, like its cousin.
  \item el cine — where you met \emph{graphein} before.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{GRA-mo}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard, and \emph{gr} is one cluster. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el gramo} — \textquotedblleft{}the gram.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{grámma} is what has been written — a letter, a mark, a scratch — from \textbf{gráphein}, to scratch or write. You met \emph{gráphein} in \emph{el cine}, inside the \emph{cinematógrafo}.

It also named a very small unit of weight, because a small weight is a scratch on a balance beam. That is the one the metric system picked up.

Which means \textbf{el gramo} and \textbf{la gramática} are the same Greek word. Grammar is the art of letters; a gram is a written mark on a scale. Nothing else connects them.

The same \emph{gramma} is all over Spanish and English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el programa} — written in advance;
  \item \textbf{el diagrama} — written across;
  \item \textbf{el telegrama} — written far;
  \item \textbf{anagram} — written back;
  \item \textbf{epigram} — written on.
\end{itemize}

And a Spanish note worth keeping: \emph{el programa}, \emph{el diagrama} and \emph{el telegrama} all end in \emph{-a} and are all masculine, because Greek neuters in \emph{-ma} came into Spanish that way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The unit of weight, and a Greek word that turns out to be underneath grammar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el gramo}
  \item \emph{cien gramos}
  \item \emph{un gramo y un metro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{grámma} mean? (Something written.) And which everyday word for the rules of a language is the same root? (Grammar.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el kilo]{el kilo — the Greek thousand, not the Latin one}

\label{lesson:ES-C359-kilo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the metre}, then \emph{the gram}. (\emph{El metro}; \emph{el gramo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item mil gracias — the other thousand.
  \item el gramo — what it counts a thousand of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KI-lo}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{k} is hard; this is one of the few Spanish words that keeps a \emph{k} at all. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el kilo} — \textquotedblleft{}the kilo.\textquotedblright{}

The men who built the metric system made one tidy decision: the prefixes that make a unit \textbf{bigger} come from Greek, and the ones that make it \textbf{smaller} come from Latin.

So \emph{kilo-}, \emph{hecto-} and \emph{deca-} are Greek, and \emph{deci-}, \emph{centi-} and \emph{mili-} are Latin. You can read a metric word and know which way it is going before you know what it means.

\textbf{Kilo-} is Greek \textbf{khīlioi}, a thousand. A \emph{kilogramo} is a thousand \emph{gramos}; a \emph{kilómetro} is a thousand \emph{metros}. Spanish clips both in ordinary speech and says \emph{un kilo}, \emph{diez kilos}.

And here is what it is \textbf{not}. Latin's thousand is \textbf{mille}, and you already have it: it is the \emph{mil} in \emph{mil gracias}. English keeps \emph{mille} in \textbf{mile}, which is \emph{mille passūs}, a thousand paces, and in \textbf{million}, a big thousand.

Two languages, two thousands, and no relation between them at all — which is why \emph{kilo} and \emph{mil} look nothing alike.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The unit you buy food in, and a rule of thumb for reading every other metric word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el kilo}
  \item \emph{un kilo de arroz}
  \item \emph{dos kilos}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language does \emph{kilo-} come from? (Greek.) And which thousand is the \emph{mil} of \emph{mil gracias}? (The Latin one, \emph{mille}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el litro]{el litro — the same word as the pound}

\label{lesson:ES-C359-litro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the gram}, then \emph{the kilo}. (\emph{El gramo}; \emph{el kilo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el agua — what it measures most often.
  \item la cantidad — the plain word for how much.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LI-tro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{l} is clear, and \emph{tr} is one cluster. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el litro} — \textquotedblleft{}the litre.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Lítra} was a unit of weight in Greek Sicily, and Latin borrowed it as \textbf{lībra}, the pound. So the \emph{litro} in a bottle and the \emph{libra} on an old set of scales are one word that split in two: French took the Greek shape for the new metric measure, and Spanish took that from French.

The Latin half is hiding all over English, and nobody sees it because it is never spelled the way it sounds:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a pound is abbreviated \textbf{lb} — that is \emph{lībra}, not \emph{pound};
  \item \textbf{Libra} is the scales in the sky, the constellation shaped like a balance;
  \item to \textbf{deliberate} is \emph{dē-lībrāre}, to weigh a thing thoroughly before deciding;
  \item \textbf{equilibrium} is equal weights;
  \item and a \textbf{level} is a \emph{lībella}, a little balance.
\end{itemize}

Spanish kept \emph{la libra} for the pound as well, so both halves of the split are still in the language, one in the kitchen and one in the history books.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The unit you buy liquid in, and an old weight hiding inside five English words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el litro}
  \item \emph{un litro de agua}
  \item \emph{dos litros de agua}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word is \emph{litro} a twin of? (\emph{Lībra}, the pound.) And why is a pound written \emph{lb}? (From \emph{lībra}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el peso]{el peso — the weight that turned into money}

\label{lesson:ES-C359-peso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the kilo}, then \emph{the litre}. (\emph{El kilo}; \emph{el litro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item contar — the other way to find out how much.
  \item la moneda — what took its name from it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PE-so}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{s} is clear, never buzzed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el peso} — \textquotedblleft{}the weight.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pendere} meant two things at once: to hang, and to weigh. That is not two meanings — it is one, because the way you weighed a thing was to hang it from a balance. \textbf{Pēnsum} is what came off the scale: a portion, weighed out.

Then money got involved. Before coins were trusted, you paid in metal and you weighed it, so paying and weighing became one act. English is still full of the consequences:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{pension} is a payment weighed out at intervals;
  \item to \textbf{spend} is \emph{expendere}, to weigh out;
  \item something \textbf{expensive} cost a lot of weighing;
  \item to \textbf{compensate} is to weigh one thing against another.
\end{itemize}

The hanging survived too, in a \textbf{pendant} and a \textbf{pendulum}, both of which dangle. And to \textbf{ponder} is \emph{ponderāre}, to weigh a thing in your mind — which is also what \textbf{pensive} does.

Spanish then named a coin after the weight and shipped it across an ocean, which is why so much of the Americas still counts in \textbf{pesos}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A length, a weight and a volume, all with a number in front: \emph{el metro}, \emph{el gramo}, \emph{el kilo}, \emph{el litro}, \emph{el peso}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el peso}
  \item \emph{el peso del pan}
  \item \emph{un kilo, un litro, un metro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things did \emph{pendere} mean? (To hang and to weigh.) And why is a coin called \emph{un peso}? (It was named after the weight of metal.)
\end{tcolorbox}
